passage: Damini had been going to bed at three for months, and the maths exam was three weeks away. Jumping to ten at night would only mean lying awake, so she chose small steps. Asif, her classmate, agreed to phone at seven every morning so her wake-up time stayed fixed. Bedtime went to quarter to three for three days, then half past two, then quarter past, then two. On the ninth night a wedding band began playing drums in the next lane and she almost gave up the plan. She kept the wake-up time anyway, was tired the next day, and held the step. Twelve days later she was asleep by two and waking without the call. It was not ten yet, but it was moving.

qa.q: What time did Asif phone Damini each morning?
qa.a: Asif phoned at seven every morning.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling on the ninth night, and what did she do?
qa.a: Damini felt tempted to give up because of the wedding drums, but she kept the wake-up time and held the step.

qa.q: What else could Damini do to keep moving towards an earlier bedtime, and why?
qa.a: Damini could keep a lamp-off routine and dim screens before each new step, because a steady wind-down makes the earlier time easier to keep.

qa.q: How might Asif see the morning calls?
qa.a: Asif probably sees them as a small way to help a classmate before the exam and is pleased when the calls are no longer needed.

grounding: Instead of jumping from 3 am to 10 pm, the student moves bedtime earlier by fifteen minutes every few days, keeping a fixed wake-up time so the body clock adjusts steadily.

passage:
For a month, Chinmay had been falling asleep at 3 am in their Thane flat, scrolling or studying, and dragging himself to school on four hours of sleep.

His sister Ira had tried jumping straight to a 10 pm bedtime once. "I lay awake till two," she told him. "Total waste. Go slow."

So he made a plan on a sticky note on the fridge. Alarm at 6:30 every day, even Sunday. Bedtime: 2:45 this week. Then 2:30. Then 2:15. Fifteen minutes earlier every three or four days.

The first week felt pointless. By week three he was in bed at 1:30 and actually sleeping. By week six it was 11:45, and his head no longer felt full of cotton in first period.

"Not ten yet," Ira said, reading the note.

"No," Chinmay said. "But I'm not lying awake either."

qa.q: What time did Chinmay's alarm go off every day?
How did Chinmay feel about the plan in the first week?
qa.a: He felt doubtful and a bit impatient, because the change seemed too small to matter.

qa.q: What else could Chinmay add to help the new bedtime stick?
qa.a: He could dim the lights and put the phone away half an hour before each new bedtime, so his body gets a clear signal to slow down.

qa.q: How might Ira see her brother's progress?
qa.a: Ira likely feels quietly pleased and a little proud, since her 'go slow' advice from her own failed attempt worked for him.

grounding: Shows a student moving bedtime earlier by fifteen minutes every few days while keeping a fixed wake time, instead of jumping from 3 am to 10 pm.

passage:
"You're going to bed at nine tonight?" Kalyani asked, leaning in Tanvir's bedroom doorway. "Last night you slept at three."

"Exams in two months. I have to fix it."

"You'll just stare at the ceiling. Remember when Papa tried that?"

Tanvir sighed. "So what, then?"

"Same wake-up every day. Seven. Even weekends. Then go to bed fifteen minutes earlier every few days."

"Fifteen minutes? That'll take forever."

"Twelve weeks, maybe less. Faster than failing every night and giving up."

Tanvir took a pen. "Okay. Tonight 2:45. Wake at seven."

Three weeks later, Kalyani passed the door at 12:40 and the light was already off. At breakfast Tanvir was eating properly, not just gulping tea.

"How's the ceiling?" she teased.

"Boring," Tanvir said. "I'm asleep before I can look at it."

qa.q: What wake-up time did they agree on?
How did Tanvir feel about the fifteen-minute steps at first?
qa.a: Tanvir felt impatient and doubtful, thinking it would take forever.

qa.q: What else could help Tanvir once bedtime is closer to midnight?
qa.a: A short wind-down routine, like dim lights and no screens for the last half hour, could make each new bedtime easier to keep.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel seeing the light off at 12:40?
qa.a: Kalyani probably feels pleased and a little proud of her advice, and relieved that Tanvir is finally sleeping.

grounding: Shows a student moving bedtime earlier in small steps while keeping a fixed wake time, rather than jumping straight to an early bedtime.
